# Overview

The [linear regression vignette](using-rcppensmallen.html) and the
[logistic regression vignette](logistic-regression.html) both hand
[`ensmallen`](https://www.ensmallen.org/docs.html) a class carrying
`Evaluate()` and `Gradient()`. Their objectives are differentiable everywhere,
so the gradient is available in closed form and the optimizer can be chosen for
speed.

Least absolute deviations regression removes that choice. Its objective is a
sum of absolute values, and an absolute value has no derivative at zero. The
zeros are not an edge case to be routed around: a least absolute deviations fit
puts residuals exactly on zero, so the objective has no gradient at the point
the optimizer is looking for. What follows from that is which member functions
the C++ class can supply, and which optimizers will accept it.

The C++ below is a fragment of one file, which ships with the package as
`src/example-lad-gradient-free.cpp` and is compiled into it as
`lad_reg_pso()`. Because compiling C++ is slow, this vignette displays the
source without rebuilding it and calls the precompiled function to produce the
numbers.

```{r setup}
library(RcppEnsmallen)
```

# The objective

The design matrix is $\mathbf{X} \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times p}$ with entries
$X_{ij}$, the coefficient vector is $\beta \in \mathbb{R}^{p}$, and the
response $\mathbf{y} \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is continuous. Indices run
$i = 1, \dots, n$ over observations and $j = 1, \dots, p$ over coefficients. An
intercept is a column of ones inside $\mathbf{X}$ rather than a separate term.

The residual vector collects the $n$ discrepancies between the response and the
fit:

$$r(\beta) = \mathbf{y} - \mathbf{X}\beta \in \mathbb{R}^{n}, \qquad r_i(\beta) = y_i - \sum_{j=1}^{p} X_{ij}\,\beta_j$$

Least squares sums the squares of those residuals. Least absolute deviations
sums their absolute values, which collapses the $n$ of them to one number the
same way:

$$f(\beta) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \lvert r_i(\beta) \rvert = \lVert \mathbf{y} - \mathbf{X}\beta \rVert_1 \in \mathbb{R}$$

The two losses treat a distant point differently. Doubling a residual doubles
its contribution to $f$ and quadruples its contribution to the residual sum of
squares, so a response far from the fitted line pulls a least squares fit
toward itself with a force that grows as it moves away, and pulls a least
absolute deviations fit with a force that does not. That is the reason to
minimize $f$ at all: it is the fit for data whose errors have heavy tails.

# Where the derivative goes missing

The absolute value has derivative $\mathrm{sign}(u)$ for $u \neq 0$ and no
derivative at $u = 0$, where the left and right slopes are $-1$ and $+1$. At a
$\beta$ that leaves every residual away from zero the chain rule applies term by
term, and $\partial r_i / \partial \beta_j = -X_{ij}$ gives

$$\frac{\partial f}{\partial \beta_j} = -\sum_{i=1}^{n} X_{ij}\,\mathrm{sign}\left(r_i(\beta)\right), \qquad j = 1, \dots, p$$

$$\nabla f(\beta) = -\mathbf{X}^{\top}\mathrm{sign}\left(r(\beta)\right) \in \mathbb{R}^{p}$$

That expression is defined on a set that excludes the answer. A least absolute
deviations fit for a design with $p$ columns passes exactly through $p$ of the
observations, so $p$ of its residuals are zero and the gradient above is
undefined there. The [verification](#verifying-the-result) below counts those
residuals on the fitted model, and the second panel of the figure shows the
kink they produce.

A `Gradient()` written from that formula would be undefined at the solution,
and away from it would return a vector whose length does not shrink as the fit
improves: $\mathrm{sign}$ reports plus or minus one however small a residual
gets. A gradient method reads a vanishing gradient as convergence, and this one
does not vanish. The class therefore supplies the objective and stops.

# The arbitrary function contract

`ensmallen` sorts objectives by which member functions they define, and each
optimizer states which of those sets it can work with. A class carrying
`Evaluate()` alone is an
[arbitrary function](https://www.ensmallen.org/docs.html#arbitrary-functions).

| Contract | Member functions |
|---|---|
| Arbitrary | `Evaluate()` |
| Differentiable | `Evaluate()`, `Gradient()` |
| Differentiable separable | `Evaluate()` and `Gradient()` over a batch, `NumFunctions()`, `Shuffle()` |
| Constrained | `Evaluate()`, `Gradient()`, `NumConstraints()`, `EvaluateConstraint()`, `GradientConstraint()` |

Reading down the table, the contracts get more demanding and the set of
optimizers that accept them gets smaller. The first row asks for the least and
is the row this vignette sits on; the [logistic regression
vignette](logistic-regression.html) writes the second and third, and the
[constrained optimization vignette](constrained-optimization.html) writes the
fourth.

Every standalone file using `RcppEnsmallen` opens with the same two lines. The
attribute tells `Rcpp::sourceCpp()` where to find the headers.

```{Rcpp header, eval = FALSE}
#include <RcppEnsmallen.h>
// [[Rcpp::depends(RcppEnsmallen)]]
```

The class holds the data and computes one number from a coefficient vector.

```{Rcpp classdef, eval = FALSE}
// Define an arbitrary objective function by implementing Evaluate() and
// nothing else.
class LADFunction
{
public:
    // Construct the object with the given design matrix and responses.
    LADFunction(const arma::mat& X,
                const arma::vec& y) :
    X(X), y(y) { }

    // Return the objective function for model parameters beta.
    double Evaluate(const arma::mat& beta)
    {
        return arma::accu(arma::abs(y - X * beta));
    }

private:
    // The design matrix.
    const arma::mat& X;
    // The responses to each data point.
    const arma::vec& y;
};
```

`y - X * beta` is the $n \times 1$ residual vector, `arma::abs()` acts on it
elementwise, and `arma::accu()` sums the result to the single number
`Evaluate()` returns. `beta` arrives as a $p \times 1$ matrix, one entry per
column of `X`, as it does in the differentiable classes.

# What the compiler says when the contract is wrong

The pairing between a class and an optimizer is checked when the file is
compiled, not when it runs. Substituting
[`ens::CMAES<>`](https://www.ensmallen.org/docs.html#cma-es) for the optimizer
used below and rebuilding gives three errors, of which these two carry the
information. File paths, line numbers and the instantiation traces between
them are cut, and the long lines are wrapped:

```
error: no member named 'NumFunctions' in 'LADFunction'
   const size_t numFunctions = function.NumFunctions();

error: static assertion failed due to requirement
'CheckSeparableEvaluate<LADFunction, arma::Mat<double>,
arma::Mat<double>>::value': The FunctionType does not have a correct
definition of Evaluate(). Please check that the FunctionType fully satisfies
the requirements of the ArbitrarySeparableFunctionType API; see the optimizer
tutorial for more details.
```

The second message names the contract CMA-ES wants, which is the arbitrary
*separable* one: `Evaluate()` taken over a batch of data points, plus a
`NumFunctions()` reporting how many there are. That is a different row of the
table above from the one `LADFunction` sits on, and the first message is the
missing member function stated outright.

The static checks live in
`inst/include/ensmallen_bits/function/static_checks.hpp`, and each contract has
its own message there naming itself. A build failure therefore identifies the
API the optimizer expects without any need to look the optimizer up first.

# Running the optimizer

[`ens::LBestPSO`](https://www.ensmallen.org/docs.html#pso) is a local best
particle swarm optimizer. It scatters candidate coefficient vectors across the
search space and moves each one toward the best point it has seen and the best
point its neighbors have seen, using nothing but the objective values it
collects along the way.

```{Rcpp ladpso, eval = FALSE}
// [[Rcpp::export]]
arma::vec lad_reg_pso(const arma::mat& X, const arma::vec& y) {

    // Construct the objective function.
    LADFunction ladf(X, y);

    // Create the local best particle swarm optimizer with default parameters.
    // The ens::LBestPSO type can be replaced with any ensmallen optimizer that
    // can handle arbitrary functions, meaning ones that supply Evaluate()
    // alone.
    ens::LBestPSO pso;

    // Create a starting point for our optimization. The swarm is placed at
    // random, so only the shape of this matrix is read. The model has p
    // parameters, so the shape is p x 1.
    arma::mat beta(X.n_cols, 1, arma::fill::zeros);

    // Run the optimization. The swarm draws through R's random number
    // generator, so set.seed() on the R side pins the result.
    pso.Optimize(ladf, beta);

    return beta;
}
```

Only the shape of `beta` reaches the optimizer. The swarm is initialized at
random, so the zeros are read for their dimensions and then overwritten, which
is a departure from the L-BFGS examples where the starting values are the point
the search begins at.

The file shipped with the package adds a block of `Rcpp::stop()` argument
checks at the top of this function, omitted here so the optimizer setup stays
in view. Those checks reject a non-finite `X` or `y`, since a single `NA` makes
the objective non-finite for every particle, leaving the swarm with nothing to
move toward and the untouched starting point coming back as if it were a fit.
The response is continuous here, so the check on `y` is finiteness rather than
the membership in $\{0, 1\}$ the logistic examples require.

**Note:** the class definition and the exported function must live in the same
C++ file.

# Verifying the result

The simulation draws its errors from a $t$ distribution with two degrees of
freedom, which has no finite variance, since heavy tails are the setting this
loss is for.

```{r data-generation}
n <- 400
beta <- c(2, -1.5, 0.8)
p <- length(beta)

set.seed(512)

# Design matrix with an intercept column
X <- cbind(1, matrix(rnorm(n * (p - 1)), ncol = p - 1))

# Continuous responses with heavy tailed errors
y <- as.vector(X %*% beta + rt(n, df = 2))
```

`optim(method = "Nelder-Mead")` is the base R comparison. It is the natural
one: like the particle swarm it never asks for a derivative, so both solvers
are working with the same information about the same surface.

```{r estimation}
obj <- function(b) sum(abs(y - X %*% b))

set.seed(512)
fit <- lad_reg_pso(X, y)

nm <- optim(rep(0, p), obj, method = "Nelder-Mead",
            control = list(maxit = 20000, reltol = 1e-12))
```

```{r comparison-table, echo = FALSE}
compare_coefs <- cbind(beta, as.vector(fit), nm$par)
colnames(compare_coefs) <- c("Truth", "LBestPSO", "Nelder-Mead")
rownames(compare_coefs) <- paste0("Beta", seq_len(nrow(compare_coefs)))
knitr::kable(compare_coefs, digits = 6, longtable = FALSE,
             caption = "Comparison of Estimated Coefficients")
```

The two solvers agree to three decimal places, and each sits further from the
truth than from the other, which is the expected outcome: the gap to the
generating parameters is sampling error at $n = 400$ with $t_2$ noise, not
optimizer error.

```{r agreement}
max(abs(as.vector(fit) - nm$par))
```

Coefficients are the loose measure here. A piecewise linear surface is flat
along the directions that move a coefficient without moving any residual across
zero, so two solvers can stop at visibly different points of the same flat
region. The objective is the tight measure, and it is also the one being
minimized:

```{r objective}
c(LBestPSO = obj(fit), NelderMead = nm$value)

obj(fit) - nm$value
```

The swarm reaches the lower value of the two. Nelder-Mead closes the remaining
gap when it is restarted from its own answer until it stops improving, which is
the reference the package tests measure against; a single call from a vector of
zeros stops short.

The $p$ zero residuals asserted earlier are visible in the fit:

```{r residuals}
resid <- as.vector(y - X %*% fit)
sort(abs(resid))[1:5]
```

The three smallest, one per column of `X`, fall below 1e-9, and the fourth is
larger than the third by seven orders of magnitude. The fitted plane passes
through three of the four hundred points exactly, and the objective has no
derivative there.

The formula that a `Gradient()` would have used behaves as described. Its
length at the fit is of order one rather than of order zero, and stepping a
millionth of a unit away does not shrink it.

```{r nonvanishing}
grad <- function(b) -as.vector(t(X) %*% sign(as.vector(y - X %*% b)))

set.seed(9)
step <- rnorm(p)
step <- step / sqrt(sum(step^2))

c(at_the_fit = sqrt(sum(grad(fit)^2)),
  a_step_away = sqrt(sum(grad(fit + 1e-6 * step)^2)))
```

An optimizer watching that number for a signal to stop would wait forever.

Plotting the objective against one coefficient shows what that means for an
optimizer. Holding the first and third coefficients at their fitted values and
varying the second gives a one-dimensional slice, drawn twice: over a wide
window beside the squared-error loss on the same data, and magnified around the
minimum.

```{r kink-plot, fig.width = 6.8, fig.height = 3.4, fig.alt = "Two panels. The left panel plots the absolute and squared error objectives against the second coefficient over a window three units wide, both rescaled to a common range; the two curves are bowl shaped and nearly indistinguishable near the bottom. The right panel magnifies the absolute error objective around its minimum, where it is a chain of straight segments joined at marked breakpoints, with a sharp corner at the minimum rather than a smooth turn."}
hold <- X[, 1] * fit[1] + X[, 3] * fit[3]
l1 <- function(b2) sum(abs(y - hold - X[, 2] * b2))
sse <- function(b2) sum((y - hold - X[, 2] * b2)^2)

op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4.1, 4.3, 3.1, 1.1))

# Left: both losses over a wide window, each shifted to its own minimum and
# scaled to a common range so they share an axis.
wide <- seq(fit[2] - 1.5, fit[2] + 1.5, length.out = 400)
rescale <- function(v) (v - min(v)) / diff(range(v))
plot(wide, rescale(vapply(wide, l1, 0)), type = "l", lwd = 2, col = "#1b6ca8",
     ylim = c(0, 1), xlab = expression(beta[2]),
     ylab = "Objective, rescaled", main = "Both losses")
lines(wide, rescale(vapply(wide, sse, 0)), lwd = 2, col = "#c0392b", lty = 2)
legend("top", bty = "n", cex = 0.8, legend = c("Absolute", "Squared"),
       col = c("#1b6ca8", "#c0392b"), lty = c(1, 2), lwd = 2)

# Right: the absolute loss near the minimum. A kink sits at every b2 that
# sends one residual through zero.
kinks <- (y - hold) / X[, 2]
halfw <- sort(abs(kinks - fit[2]))[8]
near <- kinks[abs(kinks - fit[2]) <= halfw]
zoom <- seq(fit[2] - halfw, fit[2] + halfw, length.out = 1500)
plot(zoom, vapply(zoom, l1, 0), type = "n", xlab = expression(beta[2]),
     ylab = "Sum of absolute residuals", main = "Absolute, magnified")
abline(v = near, col = "grey80", lty = 3)
lines(zoom, vapply(zoom, l1, 0), lwd = 2, col = "#1b6ca8")
points(near, vapply(near, l1, 0), pch = 16, cex = 0.7, col = "#1b6ca8")
points(fit[2], l1(fit[2]), pch = 4, cex = 1.7, lwd = 2, col = "#c0392b")
par(op)
```

At the scale of the left panel both curves look like smooth bowls that meet at
the bottom, and either one looks like something a gradient method could
descend.
The right panel covers a window a few percent as wide. The absolute loss there
is a
chain of straight segments whose slope changes at each dotted line, and each
dotted line is a value of $\beta_2$ that sends one residual through zero. The
minimum, marked with a cross, is a corner rather than a smooth turn: the slope
arrives negative and leaves positive with nothing in between. Each break
changes the slope by $2\lvert X_{i2} \rvert$, which is why the breaks
belonging to small entries of the second column are hard to see.

# Choosing among the gradient-free optimizers

Five optimizers in `ensmallen` accept a class shaped like `LADFunction`.
Swapping the type on one line of `lad_reg_pso()` is the whole change, since the
class and the call are untouched:

```{Rcpp swap, eval = FALSE}
    ens::LBestPSO pso;   // ens::SA<>, ens::CNE, ens::SPSA and ens::DE also
                         // accept a class that supplies Evaluate() alone.
```

Run at their default settings on the data generated above, each seeded with
`set.seed(512)` and started from a vector of zeros, they separate clearly. The
reference is Nelder-Mead restarted from its own answer until it stops
improving, which reaches 657.916218 on this data, and the gap column reports
how far above that each optimizer stopped.

| Optimizer | Objective | Gap to the reference |
|---|---|---|
| `ens::LBestPSO` | 657.916218 | 1.9e-10 |
| `ens::SA<>` | 657.916432 | 2.1e-04 |
| `ens::CNE` | 657.949083 | 3.3e-02 |
| `ens::SPSA` | 658.023219 | 1.1e-01 |
| `ens::DE` | 662.798752 | 4.9e+00 |

The swarm is the reason `lad_reg_pso()` uses it: it matches the reference to
2e-10 on the objective and to 3.5e-10 on the worst coefficient. Simulated
annealing lands close behind. Conventional neural evolution and simultaneous
perturbation stochastic approximation stop at points that are visibly worse but
still recognizable as the fit.

Differential evolution at its defaults misses badly, by roughly five units of
objective and 0.23 in the worst coefficient. Its own header says as much. The
constructor takes a population size, a maximum number of generations, a
crossover rate and a differential weight, and the comment above it reads that
"the default values provided over here are not necessarily suitable for a given
function" and that adjusting them to the problem is highly recommended.

Nothing in the vector it returns announces the failure. The coefficients have
the right signs and roughly the right magnitudes, and a gradient-free optimizer
leaves behind no gradient to test for flatness at the point where it stopped.
What catches it is the comparison the table performs: a second solver on the
same data, measured on the objective.

These numbers are one run on one data set, and the ordering is not a general
ranking of the five. What generalizes is the method: hold the data, the seed
and the starting point fixed, change one type, and compare the objective rather
than the coefficients.

# Seeding

The swarm is drawn through Armadillo's random number generator, which
`RcppArmadillo` routes onto R's own stream. A fixed seed therefore makes a run
reproducible exactly as it does for the mini-batch optimizer in the logistic
regression vignette:

```{r seeding}
set.seed(20260818); first  <- lad_reg_pso(X, y)
set.seed(20260818); second <- lad_reg_pso(X, y)
identical(first, second)
```

The same mechanism means a call consumes random numbers from R's stream and
shifts whatever draws follow it. Unseeded runs land at slightly different
points on the surface, and the spread widens as `X` gains columns, so every
call whose result is compared against a fixed number should be seeded.

# Where the code lives

The class and the exported function are in
`src/example-lad-gradient-free.cpp` in the package sources, together with the
argument checks omitted above and the roxygen block that produces
`?lad_reg_pso`. The [logistic regression
vignette](logistic-regression.html#moving-this-into-an-r-package) covers what
moving a standalone file into a package involves.

The [constrained optimization vignette](constrained-optimization.html) takes
the last row of the contract table, where the class supplies `Evaluate()` and
`Gradient()` and three more member functions besides.
